nameStory: This tiny crustacean doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Derocheilocaris typica. The genus name comes from Greek words meaning 'neck-lipped shrimp,' referring to the distinctive way its mouthparts are positioned on what looks like a neck-like extension.
description: Derocheilocaris typica is an incredibly tiny marine crustacean that belongs to one of the most primitive groups of crustaceans still alive today. These microscopic animals are smaller than a grain of sand, measuring less than half a millimeter long. They have elongated, worm-like bodies with a distinctive head region and live in the spaces between sand grains along coastlines. **Note: This species is extremely rare and difficult to observe without specialized equipment.**

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Impossibly small - less than 0.5mm long, requiring a microscope to see clearly, smaller than the period at the end of this sentence

idTips.label: Elongated body
idTips.description: Worm-like, cylindrical body that appears segmented under magnification, unlike the flattened or rounded shapes of other tiny beach creatures

idTips.label: Sandy habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in wet sand between high and low tide marks, never on the surface but deep within the spaces between sand grains

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves with a distinctive undulating, snake-like swimming motion when disturbed from sand samples in seawater

habitat: Lives in the interstitial spaces between sand grains on New England beaches, particularly in the zone between high and low tides. Prefers clean, well-oxygenated sand with moderate wave action along exposed coastlines. **Caution: Only one confirmed observation in New England - extremely rare and requires specialized collection techniques.**

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm, though detection requires laboratory analysis of sand samples collected from the intertidal zone.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when warmer waters may increase their metabolic activity, but still requires microscopic examination to observe.
seasonality.fall: Activity may decrease as temperatures cool, making detection even more challenging than usual.
seasonality.winter: Likely present but dormant in sand, virtually impossible to detect without specialized equipment and techniques.

funFact: These ancient crustaceans are living fossils that have remained virtually unchanged for over 400 million years, making them older than dinosaurs, and they're so primitive they're considered a separate class of crustaceans all by themselves!
confusionNotes: Could potentially be confused with other microscopic sand-dwelling creatures like copepods or ostracods, but its elongated, segmented body and primitive features distinguish it from the more rounded or flattened shapes of these other tiny crustaceans.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents an entirely separate evolutionary lineage of crustaceans called Mystacocaridans, which are so unique they form their own class - like putting them in the same category as all insects or all spiders. They're essentially the 'missing link' between marine worms and more familiar crustaceans like crabs and lobsters.
compareHints: As the only known species in its genus found in our region, Derocheilocaris typica is most similar to other interstitial crustaceans like copepods, but differs in having a more primitive body plan with less specialized appendages. Unlike copepods which have distinct body regions, this species has a more uniformly segmented, elongated form that reflects its ancient evolutionary origins.
